summary: Reports results of a survey of pseudowire and VCCV users about implementation trends, to see whether the optional Control Word could be made always mandatory. It is informational and reports what the community said.

plainLanguage.summary: A questionnaire asked network people which setting they use.

subtitle: Survey of pseudowire and VCCV implementation practices in service provider networks.

tldr.problem: Some pseudowire encapsulations have optional Control Words, but implementations vary by vendor and service provider, causing interoperability issues. Unclear whether control words could always be mandatory.
tldr.mechanism: The PWE3 working group surveyed 17 service provider and user organizations about their pseudowire and VCCV implementations, asking about encapsulations deployed, control word usage, and VCCV control channel choices.
tldr.outcome: The survey found significant deployment of pseudowires without control words across the industry, making it clear that control word-less modes cannot be deprecated in the near future. It identifies the wide variation in VCCV control channel implementation as a source of interoperability problems.

facts.label: VCCV control channel types defined
facts.value: 3 (Control Word, Router Alert Label, TTL Expiry)

today: RFC 7079 is informational and reports survey data from 2010-2011. It remains relevant as it established that control word-less pseudowire modes cannot be deprecated due to their continued widespread deployment. The survey findings informed standards discussions on whether to mandate control word support.

sections.title: The Pseudowire Encapsulation Problem
sections.content:
The IETF's Pseudowire Emulation Edge-to-Edge (PWE3) working group defined many ways to carry layer 1 and layer 2 service data over MPLS networks. Most of these encapsulations require a Control Word (CW) to carry essential information, prevent unwanted load balancing, and distinguish Operations, Administration and Maintenance (OAM) traffic from regular traffic. However, some encapsulations make the Control Word optional: Ethernet Tagged Mode, Ethernet Raw Mode, PPP, HDLC, Frame Relay Port Mode, and ATM N:1 Cell Mode.

Because the Control Word is optional for these encapsulations, different vendors and service providers implement it differently. Similarly, Virtual Circuit Connectivity Verification (VCCV), which tests pseudowire health, offers three control channel types and multiple verification methods, creating seven possible combinations. This flexibility has led to interoperability problems in deployed networks.

To understand whether the Control Word could always be mandatory, the PWE3 working group conducted a survey of real-world implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: A way to deliver network traffic over MPLS has a feature that some networks use and some don't, causing problems when different networks try to connect.

sections.title: Survey Scope and Methodology
sections.content:
The survey ran from November 4, 2010 to February 25, 2011, conducted using the SurveyMonkey tool and advertised repeatedly on the PWE3 email list. Seventeen valid responses were received from major service providers and network operators including Verizon, Deutsche Telekom, France Telecom Orange, Telstra, Telecom New Zealand, and others. No equipment vendors responded; responses were limited to service providers and users to ensure implementation feedback rather than vendor capability information.

To ensure data validity, only responses with recognizable, company-affiliated email addresses were accepted, and only one response was accepted from each organization. The survey asked about pseudowire encapsulations implemented, the number of pseudowires deployed for each type, which VCCV control channels are used, which connectivity verification methods are used, and control word support for optional encapsulations. Space was also provided for open-ended feedback.
sections.plainLanguage: Real network operators answered questions about which features they use, starting in late 2010 and running for a few months.

sections.title: Pseudowire Deployment Trends
sections.content:
Ethernet-based encapsulations dominate deployment. Ethernet Tagged Mode (RFC 4448) was implemented by 76.5% of respondents, with 93,861 pseudowires deployed. Ethernet Raw Mode (RFC 4448) was used by 82.4%, with 94,231 deployed. Frame Relay 1:1 Mode (RFC 4619) appeared in 41.2% of responses with 50,959 pseudowires, and ATM 1:1 Mode (RFC 4717) was in 17.6% with 70,103 deployed. Specialized modes like SAToP (Structure-Agnostic TDM over Packet), CESoPSN, and TDMoIP each represented 11.8% of responses.

Most other encapsulations had limited adoption. PPP appeared in 11.8% of responses but only 500 deployed pseudowires. HDLC was in just 5.9% of implementations with zero deployed. Several encapsulations, including CEP and ATM AAL5 PDU Mode, reported zero deployment. This shows that while the PWE3 standards define many encapsulations, a few high-volume modes drive actual deployment.
sections.plainLanguage: Ethernet and Frame Relay are what networks actually use the most. Other modes exist but are rarely deployed.

sections.title: VCCV Control Channel and Verification Adoption
sections.content:
VCCV offers three control channel types: Type 1 uses the pseudowire Control Word, Type 2 uses a Router Alert Label, and Type 3 uses TTL expiration. For Ethernet modes, Type 1 was used by most respondents (7 for Tagged Mode, 8 for Raw Mode), while Types 2 and 3 each had 3-4 respondents. For other encapsulations, adoption was sparse: only 1 respondent used Type 1 for SAToP, PPP reported zero use of any type, and Frame Relay modes showed mixed choices.

For connectivity verification methods, LSP Ping dominated. Ethernet Tagged and Raw modes reported 11 uses of LSP Ping versus 5-6 ICMP Ping uses. Most other encapsulations showed only LSP Ping usage or zero adoption. This indicates a clear preference for VCCV's label-based verification method over ICMP, though some respondents combined both approaches.
sections.plainLanguage: Networks pick different ways to check if their connections are working. Most pick the label-based way (LSP Ping), but some use ICMP.

sections.title: Control Word Optionality and Interoperability Findings
sections.content:
A critical finding: For encapsulations where the Control Word is optional, vendor support and actual use diverge significantly. Ethernet Tagged Mode showed 13 respondents with vendor/network support for the Control Word, but only 6 actually used it. Ethernet Raw Mode had 14 supporting it but only 7 using it. PPP had 5 vendors supporting Control Word but zero network usage. Frame Relay Port Mode showed 3 with support and 1 using it; ATM N:1 Cell Mode had 5 with support and 1 using it.

The survey identified serious interoperability challenges through user feedback. Respondents noted that VCCV traffic does not always follow the same path as customer traffic, making health checks unreliable. Multi-vendor networks struggle with incompatible VCCV implementations, leading to reduced operational efficiency. Some vendors implement VCCV only with Control Word mandatory, creating deployment obstacles. Users strongly preferred an in-band method using the Control Word for consistency across vendors.

The most important conclusion: the widespread deployment of pseudowires without Control Words means control word-less modes cannot be deprecated soon. This mandates continued support for optional Control Word encapsulations and their VCCV variants.
sections.plainLanguage: Vendors build in support for control words but networks don't always use them. When networks from different vendors connect, features don't match, causing problems. This means old ways have to keep working.
